unit.title: Support continuous improvement systems and processes

summary: This unit teaches you to help an electrical contractor get steadily better at what it does. You will learn the PDCA cycle, how to measure a starting point, how to find root causes with check sheets, Pareto charts, fishbone diagrams and the 5 whys, how to spot waste and organise a workplace with 5S, how to choose, trial and standardise improvements, and how to involve the crew, handle resistance and record lessons, without ever trading away safety or testing.

blocks.p: Every electrical contractor has jobs that run late, materials that go missing, forms with mistakes and clients who call back. **Continuous improvement** means finding such problems in a regular, planned way, trying better methods on a small scale, measuring whether they work, and keeping the ones that do. It is not a campaign or a one-off project: when one improvement is done, the team looks for the next. As a Level 3 lead electrician you are the person who sees the problems first, and who must turn good ideas into changes the whole crew uses.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Say what it is, why small steady changes work, and how a system differs from a one-off fix.
Plan a change from data, trial it on a small scale, check the results against the starting point, then standardise or adjust.
Take a baseline, choose simple measures, keep check sheets, draw run charts and work out percentage changes and payback.
Use Pareto charts, fishbone diagrams and the 5 whys to get past symptoms to causes you can fix.
Cut waste and organise the workplace
Spot the kinds of waste in electrical work and apply 5S to vans, stores and workshops.
Compare ideas on benefit, cost, effort and risk; reject any that remove a safety step; run a trial.
Collect ideas from the crew, give feedback on every one, explain changes, and deal with resistance.
Write the improved method into the procedure, train the crews, withdraw old copies, and record lessons so others can use them.
Set a review date, check the change is used, chart the results and decide whether it has worked.

blocks.note: Improvement means doing the job **better**, never doing less of what keeps people safe. Safe isolation, proving dead, testing every circuit and keeping supervision are not 'waste' to be cut. If an idea saves time by removing a safety step, a test or a check, the answer is no. Then ask the better question: how can we do the same step faster or easier while still doing it?
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Improvement ideas are often free: a better van layout, a checklist, grouping jobs by area. Jamaican contractors work with tight margins and long travel between parishes, so savings in time, fuel and re-work add up quickly. Many Jamaican companies also meet quality-system ideas through customers or lenders who ask for documented procedures.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: What continuous improvement means and where ideas come from

head: One-off fix
Continuous improvement
rows: Finds why it happened and stops it happening again
A regular routine with a named owner
Lesson stays in one person's head
Lesson recorded and shared with every crew

ul: A small change is cheap and quick to **try**, easy to **check** and easy to reverse if it fails.
Many small gains add up: 5 minutes saved on each of 10 jobs a week is almost an hour.
Crews adopt small changes more willingly than a sudden big one.
A big change that fails can cost a lot of money and trust.

head: Source
Examples
rows: Ideas from people who do the work: a better way to label boards, a van layout, a jig for bending conduit.
Complaints and comments: dust, late arrival, unclear invoices, repeated callbacks.
Callback logs, inspection failures, job sheet hours, stock-out records.
Internal checks of records and work, and the licensed inspector's failure reports.
A worker nearly touches a live terminal on a mislabelled board: the cause is a labelling problem to fix.
New tools, better materials, methods seen elsewhere, training offers.
Comparing your results with the best (another crew, another firm, an industry figure) to find the gaps.

blocks.note: A **near miss** is an event in which nobody was hurt but someone could have been. It is a free warning. A workplace that punishes people for reporting near misses soon stops hearing about them, and the next one may kill someone. Reward reports and treat them as the best source of improvement.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Put agreed changes into practice on your crew and **report the results**.
Ask regularly what slows the crew down and what could be done better.
Collect ideas, give each one an answer, and pass good ones up.
You do not write the company's mission or set its prices; you make improvement happen on site.

blocks.p: **PDCA** (Plan, Do, Check, Act) is the basic improvement cycle. It is repeated: the end of one turn is the start of the next.

flow: Plan: study the problem with data; find the causes; plan a change and a target
Do: try the change on a small scale
Check: compare the results with the starting point and ask the crew
Act: if it works, make it the standard and train everyone; if not, adjust the plan and go round again

head: Step
What you do
Example: too many nuisance RCD trips on new houses
rows: Define the problem; collect data; find causes; choose a change; set a target, the measure and a review date

Records show 9 of the last 30 houses had nuisance trips in the first month, mostly from neutrals shared between circuits. Plan: add a neutral-and-earth insulation test to each board's checklist before handover; target: 3 or fewer in the next 30 houses.
Run the change on a small scale: one crew, a few jobs
Crew A uses the new checklist line on the next 6 houses.
Measure; compare with the baseline; ask the crew what worked and what did not
No nuisance trips on those 6 houses; the test adds 10 minutes per board. The crew say the form is awkward to fill in.
Standardise what worked (and fix what did not); then start the next cycle
The line goes into the handover checklist with a tidier layout; all crews are briefed; trips are tracked monthly for the next 30 houses.

ul: Skipping **Check**: assuming a change worked because it felt better.
Skipping the baseline, so there is nothing to compare with.
Trying the change on every site at once, so a failure is costly and the cause is unclear.
Declaring success when the numbers have not moved. If callbacks have not fallen three months after a new checklist, check that it is really being used and look for other causes.
Stopping after one turn.

blocks.p: Some companies run a formal **quality management system**, often described in international standards, that requires documented procedures, internal audits and corrective action. You do not need the standard's clause numbers for this unit. The ideas are the same: write down how the work is done, check that it is done that way, and fix the causes when it is not.
'It feels faster' is not evidence. Measure **before** the change, so that you can show afterwards whether it helped.

A **baseline** is the measured starting point before a change: for example, the average time to rough-in a house, the number of callbacks per quarter, or the percentage of test certificates with a missing reading. Take it from at least several jobs or weeks, and note how it was measured so the same method can be used afterwards.

head: Problem
Measure
Why this and not the raw count
rows: A busy quarter has more callbacks just from having more jobs. A rate allows fair comparison.
Minutes to collect a standard list of parts
Easy to repeat before and after.
Certificates with a missing reading ÷ certificates audited
Shows the share, not just a count.
Jobs finished by the agreed date ÷ jobs completed
Compares with the promise made to clients.

blocks.p: A **check sheet** is a simple form for tallying how often each type of problem happens, filled in at the time it is found, with a tally mark for each.

A **Pareto chart** puts the causes in order from most to least frequent, with a running total. It shows that a few causes usually account for most of the problems (the **Pareto principle**, or 80/20 rule: roughly 80% of the effects come from 20% of the causes). Work first on the big few.
The top two causes give 28 of the 40 defects, which is 70%. Fix them first; the 'Other' group is kept last even if it is bigger than a single cause.

A **run chart** plots a measure over time (weekly callbacks, monthly pass rate) with a target line. It shows trends: is the measure getting better, worse or just wandering? A single week or a before-and-after pair can mislead; a run of weeks tells the real story.

head: Calculation
Formula
Example
rows: Rough-in fell from 52 hours to 46 hours: saving 6 hours per house.
Callbacks fell from 16 a quarter to 12: 4 ÷ 16 = 25%.
A J$240,000 tool that saves J$20,000 a month pays back in 240,000 ÷ 20,000 = 12 months.
Pass rate rose from 80% to 92%: 12 ÷ 80 = 15% increase (12 percentage points).

blocks.note: Always divide by the **before** figure for a percentage change. A fall from 50 to 40 is 20% (10 ÷ 50), not 25% (10 ÷ 40).
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **symptom** is what you see; a **root cause** is why it happens. Fixing symptoms leads to the same problem again next month.
Ask 'why?' repeatedly (often about five times) until you reach a cause you can fix, usually a gap in a process, not one careless person.

flow: Problem: the RCD on a client's hair-salon circuit keeps tripping
Why? There is leakage current to earth on the circuit
Why? The neutral from another circuit is joined into this one at a junction box
Why? The electrician took a neutral from the nearest box instead of the circuit's own
Why? The circuit labels were missing, so he could not tell which neutral was which
Why? There is no labelling step in our handover checklist; **root cause**: a gap in the process

blocks.p: The fix is to add a labelling check to the checklist, brief the crews, and test neutral-to-earth insulation before handover. Telling one electrician to be more careful would not have fixed the cause.

blocks.h: The fishbone (cause and effect, or Ishikawa) diagram

blocks.p: The **fishbone diagram** has the **problem** written at the 'head' of the fish. The main 'bones' are groups of possible causes, and smaller bones are the specific causes. A common set of groups for site work is **People, Method, Materials, Tools and equipment, Environment, Information (drawings and instructions)**.

head: Main bone
Possible causes of 'jobs finish late'
rows: Too few people on the job
Jobs scheduled in no order, so crews drive across the parish
Only one tester for two crews
Site not ready: walls not finished
Client changes not passed on to the crew

blocks.p: The diagram does not tell you which cause is real; it gives you a complete list to check with data and the 5 whys.

flow: Check sheet: count the problems
Pareto chart: pick the biggest few
Fishbone: list the possible causes of the top one
5 whys: find the root cause
PDCA: plan, trial and check a fix

blocks.h: Problem and cause: examples in electrical work

head: Symptom
Possible root cause
Fix at the cause
rows: No torque screwdrivers; no final tug check; rushed end-of-job work
Torque screwdrivers set to the maker's value; a tug test on every conductor; time for it in the schedule.
Panel schedule not at the board when work is done; stores issue by guess
Schedule fixed inside each panel and a kit list from the schedule.
Form too long; readings written up from memory later
Simpler form; write readings at the time; audit a sample each month.
No minimum stock list for the vans
Minimum stock list and a weekly count.

blocks.note: Do not use 'human error' or 'carelessness' as a root cause. Ask why the process let the error happen and why it was not caught. A blame culture stops people reporting problems, and then you cannot fix them.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Waste, process maps and the 5S method

blocks.p: In improvement thinking, **waste** is any activity that uses time, money or effort and adds nothing the client values. The following list is often remembered as 'TIMWOODS'.

head: Waste
Meaning
Electrical example
Improvement
rows: Moving people or materials further than needed
Crews driving across the parish between jobs in no order
Group each day's jobs by area.
Cases of rarely used fittings tying up money in the store
Set minimum and maximum levels; clear slow movers.
An electrician walks back to the van six times for parts
Pack a job kit before leaving.
A crew waits for the inspector, or for materials
Book inspections early; confirm deliveries the day before; plan back-up tasks.
Making more than is needed, or too early
Cutting 200 cable lengths when 40 are needed
More work than the client needs
Writing the same readings on three forms
Re-terminating a loose neutral on a callback
Standard method; torque screwdriver; final check.
A skilled electrician is only asked to carry boxes
Ask for ideas; delegate and develop.

blocks.p: **Example.** Long off-cuts of cable are thrown away on every job. Measuring the runs from the drawings and planning the cuts reduces the waste far more than buying cheaper cable or ordering extra.

**Value-adding or not?** A step adds value if the client would pay for it: fixing the box, pulling the cable, testing. A step that does not (walking, waiting, searching, redoing) is waste, **except** necessary steps such as inspection and safe isolation, which are not waste because they protect people and prove the work.

A **flowchart** (process map) draws each step of a process in order with boxes and arrows. It lets you see every step, who does it, how long it takes and where delays, repeat work and hand-offs occur.

flow: Phone call from the client
Details written on a message slip
Slip passed to the office
Job card made
Crew assigned
Parts collected
Visit and repair
Job sheet filled in
Invoice raised

blocks.p: Walk the process, writing what really happens (not what should happen). Mark waiting and hand-offs. Often the biggest delays are between the steps, such as a slip lying on a desk for a day.

head: Step
Meaning
Van or store example
rows: Remove everything not needed in the work area
Take out broken tools and unused items; return rarely used items to the main store.
A marked place for everything; most-used items easiest to reach
Labelled bins for fittings; a shadow board for hand tools; padded place for test instruments; heavy drums low.
Wipe down the van and tools; check leads for damage and tag faulty ones.
A layout photo fixed inside the door, a stock list with minimum levels, labels.
A short weekly crew check and a monthly check by the lead, with a score sheet.

blocks.p: A **shadow board** is a board with the outline of each tool drawn on it, so a missing tool is seen at once.

**Sustain is the hardest step.** People slip back to old habits unless checks continue and results are shared. Measure the time to find items before and after: if finding a set of parts falls from 12 minutes to 5 minutes, that is (12 − 5) ÷ 12 = 58% faster, which keeps the crew interested.

blocks.note: In stores and vans, keep heavy items low, use two people for drums and heavy boxes, wear gloves for sharp off-cuts and trunking, and put scrap copper, lamps and batteries in the correct bins. Do not throw away anything without the supervisor's approval.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Many improvements help the environment as well as the company: planning routes to cut fuel, cutting off-cut waste, recycling scrap copper, collecting old lamps and batteries for proper disposal (never in the skip), and using drawings on screen instead of printing them several times.

head: Question
Why it matters
rows: Is it **safe**, and does it keep the work legal and to the specification?
If not, the answer is no, whatever the saving.
What is the **benefit**: time, money, quality, safety?
Gives the size of the prize.
What is the **cost** in money, effort and training?
Compare with the benefit; work out the payback.
What are the **risks**, and can they be controlled?
Avoid trading one problem for another.

blocks.p: With time for only one improvement this quarter, choose by comparing benefit, cost, effort and risk, not by who proposed it or what sounds modern. A simple table with a score from 1 to 5 for each question helps the team agree.

Some time-saving ideas remove a safety step or a test: checking the voltage tester on a proving unit only once a day, testing only some circuits, working without lock-off for 'small' jobs. Reject them politely and explain why, then turn them into a better question: how can we make this step quicker while still doing it every time? For example, a test sequence sheet, better lead sets or pre-printed certificates.

flow: State the problem, the baseline and the target
Write exactly what will change
Choose a small, fair trial: one crew, or a few jobs
Brief the people in the trial and say how results will be recorded
Run it for long enough to give a real answer; keep other things the same where you can
Measure the same way as the baseline
Ask the crew what worked and what did not
Decide: adopt, adjust and repeat, or drop

blocks.p: A trial can mislead. A keen crew, an easy job or a short trial can make a change look better than it really is. Compare like with like, and be cautious about results from a handful of jobs.

If the trial proves something costs more than the team's budget allows, take the data and costs to the manager, rather than buying it anyway or dropping the idea without telling anyone. A failed trial is **useful learning**: record it so nobody repeats it.
When a trial works, make it the normal way of working. A **standard operating procedure (SOP)** or work instruction is the written step-by-step method.

flow: Write the improved method into the procedure, in plain steps
Train all crews, with practice, not just an email
Withdraw and destroy old printed copies, in vans and in the office
Update forms, checklists and labels
Set a review date and a measure
Tell everyone who suggested or helped

blocks.p: **Why remove old copies?** An old printed procedure left in a van means a crew may follow the old, poorer method. Keep one controlled, current version.

blocks.note: A result that proves good (for example fewer damaged ladders after a new way of carrying them on the vans) is recorded, shared with every crew and made the standard. Keeping it within the one crew that tried it wastes it.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: They do the work every day, so they see the problems first and know the practical details.
They are far more willing to use a change they helped to shape.
A change imposed without asking often fails when nobody is watching.
Ask at each weekly meeting: 'What slowed us down this week?' and 'What could we do better?'
A **suggestion scheme**: a box, a board or a simple form or phone message.
Thank every person, record every idea, and tell them what happens to it.
Let the person with the idea help plan and run the trial and collect the results.
Share results with the whole crew on simple charts.
Recognise contributions: name the person at a meeting.

blocks.p: When Tanisha suggests colour-coded cable ties for each circuit type, the best first response is to thank her and agree a small trial. Adopting it everywhere untested, or saying 'good idea' and doing nothing, both damage trust. When the results come back, feed them to the person who suggested it: it shows ideas are valued, so more are offered. An idea that is dropped should come with a reason.

flow: Explain **why**, using facts (for example an audit found 1 in 10 certificates with a missing reading)
Show the new method; practise on a real example
Update the written procedure; remove old forms
Give a point of contact for questions
Check early use; give feedback; share early results

blocks.p: People follow a change better when they understand the reason, not just the steps. Telling only the newest staff, emailing a form and expecting everyone to cope, or leaving old and new forms side by side all cause failures.

head: Why people resist
What helps
rows: Listen; show the data on what the old way costs; let them try the new way.
Fear of looking slow, or more paperwork
Keep the new form short; practise; give time.
A genuine flaw in the new method
Take it seriously: improve the method. Their concern may be right.
Involve respected senior electricians in the trial.
Be honest about what failed; show what is different now.

blocks.p: Forcing a change with threats, leaving people out of meetings, or letting them keep the old form for ever are all poor responses. Hear their concerns, show the benefits, support them through the first few weeks, check their early work and give feedback. If someone still refuses after support, explain that the procedure is required and report it to the manager.

To keep people motivated during a long improvement project, share progress and recognise effort. Hiding results, changing targets every week and giving all the credit to the manager all do the opposite.

ul: After each improvement project or large job, hold a short review: what was planned, what happened, what went well, what went badly, what to change.
Record it on a simple **lessons-learned form**, **including what did not work**, so others can learn and not repeat mistakes.
Keep the forms in a shared, organised file or database, with headings so they can be found, not on scraps in vans or only in the memory of the lead.
Build important lessons into procedures, training and toolbox talks.
When an experienced electrician who knows a client's installation is about to retire, capture what he knows in notes and marked-up drawings, and ask others to learn from him.

blocks.p: An **audit** is a planned check of records and work against the company's system, to find whether procedures are followed. For example, an audit finds that 1 in 10 test certificates has a missing reading. The right improvement is to find why readings are missed and fix the process, not to fill in readings from memory or stop issuing certificates.
An improvement is not finished when it is introduced. It is finished when you have shown, with figures, that it works and keeps working.

flow: Record the baseline before the change
Set a target and a review date
Check that the change is really being used (look at completed forms, not just ask)
Measure regularly in the same way and plot a run chart against the baseline and target
Ask the crew and some clients what they think
At the review date compare with the target
If it works: standardise. If not: find why (not used properly, missed the real cause, too long), adjust and go round PDCA again

head: Result
What it means
What to do
rows: Better, and the form is used
Standardise; share; plan the next cycle.
Better, but few use the form
Something else may have caused the improvement
Check; do not take the credit yet.
No change, and the form is not used
The change was never really tried
Find out why; retrain; remove obstacles.
No change, and the form is used
Go back to the root cause analysis.
The change may be causing harm

blocks.p: **Worked example.** Baseline: 18 callbacks in the last six months, 3 a month. A handover checklist is introduced with the target of halving callbacks within three months. Months 1 to 3 give 2, 2 and 1: a total of 5 in three months, about 1.7 a month. (3 − 1.7) ÷ 3 = 43% reduction: close to target. Completed checklists are on file for 28 of 30 jobs. The change is working, but not yet at target; review again next quarter.

**Review dates matter.** Without one, a change is never checked and may quietly be dropped or may continue although it does not work. A review date means the results are checked and the change adjusted if needed. It does not mean the change stops on that date.

blocks.note: Always check a proposed time-saver against the specification and the company's safety rules before it is trialled. A change that is quick but unsafe has not 'worked'.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can explain continuous improvement and why small steady changes work.
I can name sources of improvement ideas, including near misses, audits and benchmarking.
I can describe the four steps of PDCA and give an electrical example of each.
I can take a baseline, choose a fair measure and explain why a rate is better than a count.
I can make a check sheet, put causes in Pareto order and work out the share of the top causes.
I can explain a run chart and work out saving, percentage change and payback.
I can use the 5 whys and a fishbone diagram to reach a root cause.
I can name the types of waste and give an electrical example and improvement for each.
I can draw a simple process map and say where delays hide.
I can apply the five steps of 5S to a van or store, and keep the improvement going.
I can compare improvement ideas on safety, benefit, cost, effort and risk, and reject an unsafe one respectfully.
I can plan and judge a trial, and say how it could mislead.
I can standardise a proven change: write it into the procedure, train, and withdraw old copies.
I can involve the crew, give feedback on ideas and recognise contributions.
I can communicate change, manage resistance and keep people motivated.
I can record lessons learned and capture the knowledge of experienced workers.
I can monitor an improvement against a baseline, target and review date.

head: Formula
Use
rows: Count of one cause ÷ total count × 100
Share of a cause in a Pareto chart

terms: 5 whys
Asking 'why?' repeatedly to get past a symptom to a root cause.
5S
Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardise, Sustain: a method of organising a workplace.
Audit
A planned check of records and work against the company's system.
Baseline
The measured starting point before a change.
Benchmarking
Comparing your results with the best to find gaps.
Check sheet
A simple form for tallying how often each problem occurs.
Continuous improvement
A regular way of finding, testing and keeping better methods.
Fishbone diagram
A cause-and-effect (Ishikawa) diagram that groups possible causes of a problem.
Near miss
An event in which nobody was hurt but someone could have been.
Pareto chart
A chart ordering causes from most to least frequent, showing the few that matter most.
PDCA
Plan, Do, Check, Act: the improvement cycle.
Process map (flowchart)
A diagram of every step of a process in order.
Root cause
The underlying reason a problem happens, which can be fixed.
Run chart
A chart of a measure over time.
Shadow board
A tool board with the outline of each tool, so a missing tool is seen at once.
Standard operating procedure (SOP)
The written step-by-step standard method for a task.
Suggestion scheme
A system for staff to put forward improvement ideas.
Waste
Any activity that uses resources and adds nothing the client values.

c1.title: Callbacks at a Falmouth contractor
c1.text: A contractor in Falmouth, Trelawny, wires small hotels and villas. Over the last quarter it logged 50 callbacks: loose terminations 21, nuisance RCD trips 13, missing circuit labels 8, damaged accessories 5 and other causes 3. The lead electrician, Ms Shelly-Ann Crooks, takes the callback data to her crew. The crew's first suggestion is to warn everyone to be more careful.

c2.title: A 5S clean-up of a van in Morant Bay
c2.text: Mr Delano Francis's crew in Morant Bay, St Thomas, spends a long time looking for parts in their van. Timing two electricians collecting a standard list of 12 items gave an average of 14 minutes. After the crew sorts the van, gives every item a marked place, builds a shadow board, and writes a stock list with minimum levels, the same collection takes 6 minutes. Two months later the van is untidy again.

c3.title: Job kits and travel in Ocho Rios
c3.text: A contractor in Ocho Rios, St Ann, finds that electricians walk back to the van up to six times a job for fittings, and that crews drive between Ocho Rios, Runaway Bay and Port Maria in no set order. A pre-packed job kit, made up from each job's materials list, is tried by one crew on 8 jobs. A J$180,000 label printer is also proposed; the manager says its saving is about J$15,000 a month.

c4.title: A new test-result form in Mandeville
c4.text: A contractor in Mandeville, Manchester, finds in an audit that 4 of 40 test certificates have a missing reading. A shorter test-result form, filled in at the board, is approved. Senior electrician Mr Winston Kerr says, 'The old way works.' Tanya, a junior electrician, suggests that circuit labels be printed from the panel schedule. Another crew member suggests testing only half the circuits on each house to save an hour.

c5.title: A handover checklist at a Savanna-la-Mar contractor
c5.text: A contractor in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland, brought in a handover checklist for new houses. In the six months before it, there were 24 callbacks (4 a month). In the three months after, callbacks were 3, 3 and 2. The checklist has been completed for 19 of the 24 houses finished in that period. Mrs Hyacinth Bryan, the lead electrician, must decide whether the checklist is working and how to keep lessons from the project.

questions.q: Putting the callbacks in Pareto order, what share do the top two causes make up?
questions.why: Loose terminations 21 + nuisance RCD trips 13 = 34 of 50, which is 34 ÷ 50 × 100 = 68%. A Pareto chart shows that two causes give about two thirds of the callbacks, so they are worked on first. 42% is only the largest cause.

questions.q: The crew's first suggestion is to warn everyone to be more careful. Why is this a weak response?
o: Warnings cost the company money in time lost from the work
It blames people and does not look at the process for causes
Crews never listen to warnings from a lead electrician
Callbacks cannot be reduced by anything the crew does
questions.why: 'Be more careful' treats the symptom and blames people. Improvement looks for why the process lets the error happen (no torque screwdrivers, no final check, no checklist) and fixes that. A blame culture also stops people reporting problems.

questions.q: Shelly-Ann asks why loose terminations keep happening, and the crew answers: no torque screwdriver on the vans; no final tug check; the end of a job is rushed. What are these?
o: Possible root causes to check against the data and fix
Excuses, which should be written up as complaints
Symptoms, which are the final result to be recorded
Proof that the loose terminations are caused by one person
questions.why: These are process causes: tools, method and time. They can be checked (are torque screwdrivers on the vans? do the forms show a tug check?) and fixed, for example with torque screwdrivers set to the maker's value and a tug test on every conductor.

questions.q: The crew trial torque screwdrivers and a tug test on 5 houses and no terminations are found loose. What should Shelly-Ann do next in the PDCA cycle?
o: Declare success and stop, because five houses show it works
Check the results against the baseline, ask the crew, then act
Cancel the trial, as the callbacks had other causes too
Repeat the trial on the same five houses to be sure
questions.why: Check compares results with the baseline and asks the crew what worked; Act then standardises if it works, with training and a procedure. Five houses is a small sample, so she keeps measuring monthly and watches the callback rate.

questions.q: By what percentage did the time to collect the 12 items fall after the 5S clean-up?
o: About 43%
About 133%
About 57%
About 8%
questions.why: Percentage reduction = (before − after) ÷ before × 100 = (14 − 6) ÷ 14 × 100 ≈ 57%. Dividing by the after figure (8 ÷ 6) gives 133%, and 43% is the share that the new time is of the old.

questions.q: Putting every item in a marked place, with the most-used items easiest to reach, is which 5S step?
o: Shine
Sort
Sustain
Set in order
questions.why: Set in order gives everything a marked, labelled place, with frequently used items easiest to reach. Sort removes what is not needed; Shine cleans and inspects; Standardise writes the rule; Sustain keeps it going.

questions.q: The van is untidy again after two months. Which 5S step was neglected?
o: Sustain: no regular checks kept the standard going
Sort: too many items were taken out of the van
Shine: the van was cleaned too often to keep it tidy
Set in order: items should not have fixed places
questions.why: Sustain is the hardest step: without a short weekly crew check, a monthly check by the lead and shared scores, people slip back to old habits. Measuring the time to find items before and after helps keep the crew interested.

questions.q: An electrician walking back to the van six times for fittings is which kind of waste, and what is a sensible improvement?
o: Waiting; book the inspector earlier in the week
Defects; use a torque screwdriver on each terminal
Motion; pack a job kit before leaving
Inventory; order half as many fittings for the van
questions.why: Unnecessary movement by people is motion waste. A job kit packed from the job's materials list before leaving the yard removes most of the trips, and it can be trialled on a few jobs and measured.

questions.q: Crews drive between Ocho Rios, Runaway Bay and Port Maria in no set order. Which change addresses this?
o: Give each crew a faster van for the longer drives
Group each day's jobs by area and plan the route
Let crews pick their own jobs each morning
Start every job an hour earlier than before
questions.why: Unnecessary transport is waste. Grouping each day's jobs by area cuts driving time and fuel without any extra cost, and it can be measured with fuel use and jobs per day.

questions.q: How long would the J$180,000 label printer take to pay for itself if it saves J$15,000 a month?
o: 12 months
15 months
6 months
18 months
questions.why: Payback = cost ÷ saving per month = 180,000 ÷ 15,000 = 12 months. The team then compares this with other ideas on benefit, cost, effort and risk, and with how long the printer will last.

questions.q: The job-kit trial on 8 jobs, by one keen crew, saved time on every job. Which caution is most sensible?
o: The result is proven, so every crew should adopt it at once
A keen crew and few jobs may make the kit look too good
The trial should have been run on every site at once
A time saving cannot be measured on only eight jobs
questions.why: A small trial by an enthusiastic crew can overstate a benefit. The team compares like with like, keeps measuring when other crews join, and then standardises the kit if the results hold.

questions.q: What share of the audited test certificates have a missing reading, and what is the best improvement action?
o: 10%; find why readings are missed and fix the process
4%; ask clients not to read their certificates closely
10%; fill in the missing readings from memory
40%; stop issuing certificates until it is sorted
questions.why: 4 ÷ 40 × 100 = 10%. The improvement fixes the cause: why are readings missed (a long form, readings written up later)? A simpler form filled in at the board, plus a monthly audit, deals with it. Filling in from memory makes the certificate false.

questions.q: Mr Kerr says, 'The old way works.' What is the best approach?
o: Force the new form on him with a warning of discipline
Let him keep the old form while the others use the new one
Leave him out of the meetings about the new form
Hear his concerns, show the audit data and invite him to trial it
questions.why: Resistance often has real reasons, and a respected senior electrician can help the change succeed. Listen, show what the old way costs, and involve him. If he still refuses after support, the procedure is required and the manager is told.

questions.q: What is the best first response to Tanya's idea of printing circuit labels from the panel schedule?
o: Thank her and agree a small trial and a way to measure it
Adopt it on every site at once, without any trial first
Tell her that labelling is not part of a junior's job
Say it is a good idea, then take no further action on it
questions.why: A small trial tests the idea, and thanking her shows ideas are valued. Dismissing an idea, or praising it and doing nothing, stops ideas coming. When results come back, tell her what happened.

questions.q: A crew member suggests testing only half the circuits on each house to save an hour. How should the lead respond?
o: Trial it on a few houses to see what happens in practice
Accept it, because an hour a house is a large saving
Reject it as it removes a check, but ask how to test faster
Let each electrician decide for themselves on each house
questions.why: Untested circuits can hide damaged cables or wiring faults, and the certificate would not be true. An idea that removes a safety step is rejected, politely, then turned into the better question: how can we test every circuit more quickly (test sequence sheet, better lead sets)?

questions.q: By what percentage did the monthly callbacks fall on average in the three months after the checklist?
o: About 33%
About 50%
About 20%
About 80%
questions.why: After: 3 + 3 + 2 = 8 in three months, about 2.67 a month. Before: 4 a month. Reduction = (4 − 2.67) ÷ 4 ≈ 33%. This is a good start, but not yet the halving that some teams target.

questions.q: The checklist was completed for only 19 of 24 houses. What should Hyacinth do?
o: Declare the checklist a success, since callbacks have fallen
Scrap the checklist, because a fifth of the crews did not use it
Find why five houses had no checklist, and what that means
Stop measuring callbacks, as the result is already clear enough
questions.why: Callbacks fell, but the change was not fully used, so the result may be partly due to other causes, and the improvement may be larger if it is used every time. Find out why the five were missed (a form problem? time pressure?) and fix that.

questions.q: An old printed copy of the pre-checklist handover procedure is still in one van. What is the risk?
o: None, because the old and new procedures are nearly the same
That crew may follow the old, poorer method
The van will be harder to keep tidy
The crew will finish jobs too quickly
questions.why: An old copy may be followed, so the improvement is lost on that crew. When a change is standardised, all old printed copies are withdrawn, and one controlled, current version is kept.

questions.q: Hyacinth wants every crew to learn from this project, including what did not work. Where should she record it?
o: On a lessons-learned form in a shared, organised file
On scraps of paper that are kept in each of the vans
In her own memory, so she can tell each crew in turn
On her personal phone, where she can find it quickly
questions.why: Lessons are only useful if others can find them. A simple form kept in a shared, searchable file or database, including what failed, lets any crew learn and not repeat mistakes, and it survives when people leave.

questions.q: A crew member tells his lead that a ladder slipped on a wet verandah, but nobody was on it. What is the best use of this report?
o: Note it as a near miss, find why it slipped, and share the lesson
Tell him to be careful, since nobody was hurt and nothing broke
Record it as an accident, and send him for a medical check
Say nothing, because the client might hear and complain about it
questions.why: An event in which nobody was hurt but someone could have been is a near miss: a free warning. Find the cause (wet surface, no foot-holder, wrong feet), fix it, share the lesson and thank the person who reported it, so more reports come.
